en.title: Divide-and-Conquer Scheduling of Sparse High-Priority Processes
en.description:
n 1-based processes form a contiguous interval. An interval of length greater than 1 may be split into two equal halves that are assigned further; alternatively, the interval may be executed directly. If it contains no high-priority process, the cost is normal_time; otherwise, the cost is priority_time×number of high-priority processes×interval length. The total time is the sum of all processor costs, not the maximum.

The input/output format was compiled by this site.
en.input: The first line contains n k normal_time priority_time, and the second line contains k high-priority indices. Original ranges: 1≤n≤10⁹ with n a power of 2, 1≤k≤min(n,100000), indices in 1..n. On this site the indices in a valid process list are distinct; the original text gives no range for the time factors, and this site uses 1..10⁹ for both.
en.output: Output the minimum total cost. An intermediate direct cost may exceed 64 bits, so use a sufficiently wide integer; do not allocate arrays proportional to n.
en.explanation: The answers are 6, 3, and 6; in the third example, the two endpoints can each be split down to single points, while the empty intervals in between are paid for.
hints: Sort the high-priority indices; let each recursive interval carry its corresponding range of indices, and use binary search to split it into left and right subranges. An empty interval returns normal_time immediately; otherwise, compare the direct cost with the sum of the optimal costs of the two halves.
